sentences.text: Bata was eleven, and he lived, for most of the year, in a ger on the summer pastures of Övörkhangai, in the middle of Mongolia.
Ger meant the round white felt tent his family lived in — a single warm room with a stove in the center and beds along the walls.
His father, Batbayar, herded horses and yaks.
His mother taught at the small school in the sum center, a two-hour drive away.
His grandmother, Odval, lived with them.
She was in her mid-sixties, and she was, everyone said, the person in the family who really knew the land.
It was late June.
In three weeks, the whole country would be watching Naadam — the summer festival of the three manly games, which were wrestling, archery, and horse racing.
Bata's family raised racing horses.
Every summer they took three or four of the fastest yearlings and two-year-olds to the smaller regional races that led up to Naadam.
This year, for the first time, Bata was allowed to help.
On the second Monday of the month, in the early morning, Odval called Bata over to the north side of the ger.
She reached up to a wooden peg by the frame and lifted down something that had been hanging there, wrapped in a soft old cloth, for as long as Bata could remember.
He had known it was a saddle.
He had not known it was for him.
She unwrapped it and set it on the low table.
It was very small — child-sized — and made of dark leather that had been used and oiled and used and oiled for a very long time.
The silver ornaments on the pommel were dulled.
There were places where the leather had been mended, carefully, with darker thread.
Odval said, "This was your great-great-grandfather's first saddle.
He rode it when he was your age.
Then his son used it.
Then his son.
Then your father.
Now you." She looked at Bata.
"You are old enough now.
This week we ride out to bring the horses in.
You will use this."
Bata picked up the saddle.
It was heavier than he expected.
The leather smelled of woodsmoke and old sweat and something else, faint and sweet, like dry hay that had been kept somewhere warm.
He turned it over.
On the underside, near where the stirrup leather attached, he could see a small mark — a rough triangle with a dot in the middle — burned into the leather with a hot iron a very long time ago.
He asked what it was.
Odval said, "That is your great-great-grandfather's mark.
He put it on everything he made himself.
He was a saddler as well as a herder.
Some things he made for the family.
Some things he made to trade.
This one he made for himself, when he was ten.
He rode it for six years.
He made bigger ones after that."
"I never met him," Bata said.
Odval said, "No.
He died before I was born.
My grandmother told me about him.
She said he was a quiet man, and a good horseman, and he made things that lasted." She tapped the saddle.
"This is a hundred and twenty years old.
It has taken five boys through their first gathering.
You will be the sixth."
They rode out at midmorning.
Odval on her old dun mare, Bata on a small brown gelding called Chuluun, which meant Stone.
Chuluun was patient and knew the way.
The saddle fit Bata almost exactly — his great-great-grandfather must have been about his size at eleven.
The stirrups needed only one hole of adjustment.
They rode east, into the long green rolling country.
The horses they were going to gather were about three hours out, at a place called the White Spring, where Batbayar had left them a week ago to graze.
Odval rode ahead and Bata followed, the way he had ridden his whole life following adults through this land.
But today felt different.
The small saddle under him made a sound he had never heard before — a soft creak of old leather, slightly different from the newer saddle he usually used.
He listened to it as they rode.
They found the horses at the White Spring a little past midday.
There were nine — three racing yearlings, two two-year-olds, and four broodmares — and they were all together, calm, drinking.
Bata and Odval let them finish and then began the slow turning-work of steering the whole small herd back to the west.
Bata rode at the rear, whistling and clicking the way his father had taught him.
The horses moved willingly.
The sun was warm on his back.
He was, for a whole hour, happier than he had ever been.
It was Odval who noticed first.
She reined in her mare and turned in the saddle and looked behind them, back to the west, back toward home.
Bata turned too.
The sky where they were going had changed.
A wall of dark grey-purple cloud, low and heavy, was building on the horizon.
It had not been there half an hour ago.
It was already big.
Odval watched it for maybe ten seconds.
Then she said, very calmly, "Bata.
We will not make it home before that hits us.
We need to think."
